newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals--Japan markets in lull as talks loom.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals--Japan markets in lull as talks loom.

text.p: Japan's physical metal markets were quiet over the past week as users and producers prepare for their annual ritual of negotiating conditions for long-term supply contracts, traders said.
In the aluminium market, premiums remained steady at $60 to $65 per tonne over LME cash prices, although one end-user said consumers were paying premiums below $60.
He agreed with traders that many end-users were largely holding to the sidelines, awaiting signs that London Metal Exchange prices were steadying after last month's declines.
He added that if benchmark three-month aluminium can hold above $1,400 a tonne through this month the market may have found a floor.
LME prices fell last month to a 2-1/2-year low of $1,305, but have since rebounded and ended Tuesday's afternoon kerb at $1,432.

Quarterly price negotiations between aluminium producers and Japanese buyers were expected toward the end of this month. Market sources said while it was too early to predict the outcome premiums would probably be settled around the $62 level set during the last round of talks.
Traders doubted the market would be significantly affected by the resumption of shipments from Venezuelan producer Venalum, which suspended exports to Japan early this year.

Shipments were resumed at stepped-up levels last month, to make up for supplies lost during the suspension, and will return to the prior level of about 7,500 tonnes per month after next March, market sources said.
"It can't be said that it won't have any effect at all on the market, but the quantity is not so great," one trade house source said.

Copper traders expected terms for next year's contracts to be mostly decided by the end of this month, after major producers such as Chile's Codelco and Zambia's ZCCM set premiums for Japan at $50 a tonne over LME cash prices.
One market source said traders continued to eye LME copper warehouse stocks, amid signs of a slowdown in the recent sharp declines to six-year lows.
He said there remained nervousness that copper withdrawn by the Chinese might soon make its way back into LME warehouses or onto the market.
"There's talk that ships carrying Chinese copper have arrived in Singapore, although it may not end up in LME warehouses," he said.

In the concentrates market, a source at a large trade house said some talks had begun on copper, with miners apparently resigned to an increase in treatment charges next year amid signs of a rising surplus in mine supplies.
With LME copper prices well below last year's levels, however, he doubted miners would swallow a large rise in charges.
At present, he said, smelters were looking for a rise of about $20 per tonne while miners were hoping to keep increases to a minimum.
